subject: Mathematics
title: The Congruent Puzzle
hook: Isha collects passport-sized photos of her friends and notices some are exactly the same size and shape—even when flipped or rotated.

slides.title: The Congruent Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Isha arranges her photo album and notices twin shapes — exact copies in every way.

slides.title: The Discovery
slides.storyContext: Isha is organizing photos for a school project. She finds two photos of the same size and shape. She overlays them — perfect match! Then she finds two photo frames: one is blue, one is red, but they are the exact same shape and size. 'These are twins!' she exclaims. Akshay joins her: 'In geometry, we call them congruent. Let me show you the rules.'
slides.inSimpleWords: When two shapes are exactly the same size and shape, they are congruent — like identical twins.

slides.title: What is Congruence?

points.text: Two figures are congruent if they have the same size and shape.
Congruent figures can be rotated, reflected, or translated (moved), but their dimensions stay the same.
If you cut out both shapes from paper, they would fit perfectly over each other.

example.problem: Are these two triangles congruent? Triangle 1 has sides 3 cm, 4 cm, 5 cm. Triangle 2 has sides 5 cm, 3 cm, 4 cm.
example.solution: Yes. Both triangles have the same three side lengths (3, 4, 5), just listed in different order. They are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Congruent shapes are identical copies — same size, same shape, no tricks.

slides.title: Isha's Photo Album Adventure
slides.storyContext: Isha pulls out a stack of old photos. Some are 4×6 cm, and some are also 4×6 cm but rotated. 'Look, Akshay! Same size, but this one is standing up and this one is sideways.' Akshay nods: 'Both are congruent. Rotation doesn't change congruence — the shape and size stay identical.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Rotating a shape does not destroy congruence — it remains identical to the original.

slides.title: Congruent Triangles

points.text: Two triangles are congruent if all three sides of one match all three sides of the other (SSS rule).
Or: if two sides and the included angle match (SAS rule).
Or: if two angles and a side match in the right way (ASA or AAS rule).

example.problem: Triangle ABC has sides AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 7 cm. Triangle PQR has sides PQ = 5 cm, QR = 6 cm, RP = 7 cm. Are they congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by SSS (Side-Side-Side). All three sides match.

slides.inSimpleWords: To prove two triangles are congruent, check that their sides or sides-and-angles match.

slides.title: SSS Rule in Action
slides.storyContext: Isha cuts out two triangles from cardstock. Triangle 1: sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm. Triangle 2: sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm. She overlays them and they match perfectly.

example.problem: Prove Triangle 1 and Triangle 2 are congruent using SSS.
example.solution: All three sides are equal: 5 cm = 5 cm, 6 cm = 6 cm, 7 cm = 7 cm. By SSS, the triangles are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: SSS means all three sides match — if that's true, the triangles are congruent.

slides.title: SAS Rule (Side-Angle-Side)

points.text: Two triangles are congruent if two sides and the angle between them (the included angle) match.
The angle MUST be between the two sides for the rule to work.
Example: Side 5 cm, Angle 60°, Side 6 cm matches the other triangle's Side 5 cm, Angle 60°, Side 6 cm.

example.problem: Triangle A: sides 4 cm, 5 cm with a 45° angle between them. Triangle B: sides 4 cm, 5 cm with a 45° angle between them. Congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by SAS. Two sides and the included angle are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: SAS: if two sides and the angle between them match, the triangles are congruent.

slides.title: Akshay's Angle Challenge
slides.storyContext: Akshay draws two triangles. 'Isha, look at this. Triangle 1 has two sides of 6 cm and 8 cm with a 50° angle between them. Triangle 2 also has 6 cm and 8 cm with 50° between them. Are they congruent?' Isha thinks and says: 'Yes! The included angle is the same, so by SAS, they are congruent.'
slides.inSimpleWords: SAS is powerful — knowing two sides and their angle is enough to prove congruence.

slides.title: ASA Rule (Angle-Side-Angle)

points.text: Two triangles are congruent if two angles and the side between them (included side) match.
The side MUST be between the two angles.
If Angle 1 = Angle 1', Side = Side', Angle 2 = Angle 2', then triangles are congruent.

example.problem: Triangle C: Angle 50°, Side 7 cm, Angle 60°. Triangle D: Angle 50°, Side 7 cm, Angle 60°. Congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by ASA. Two angles and the included side are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: ASA: two angles and the side between them — that's congruence.

slides.title: Akshay's SSS Challenge
slides.storyContext: Akshay asks Isha: 'If I tell you a triangle has three sides of 5, 6, and 7 cm, can you draw another triangle that's NOT congruent to it?' Isha thinks: 'No! If all three sides are the same, the triangle must be congruent to the original. That's the SSS rule!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The SSS rule guarantees congruence — you cannot build a different triangle with the same three side lengths.

slides.title: Comparing Different Triangle Rules
slides.storyContext: Isha learns the triangle rules: SSS (all sides), SAS (two sides + angle), ASA (two angles + side), AAS (two angles + non-included side). Akshay says: 'Each rule is a shortcut — you don't need to check everything, just these key measurements.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Triangle congruence rules are shortcuts — knowing specific measurements is enough.

slides.title: Which Rule Applies?
slides.storyContext: Isha has Triangle P: sides 4, 5, 6. Triangle Q: angle 30°, side 4, angle 50°. Can she prove they're congruent? No—she has different information.

example.problem: To prove Triangle P ≅ Triangle Q, what info would you need?
example.solution: You'd need matching side lengths OR matching angles with a side. Different types of info cannot be mixed across triangles.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the right rule for the information you have.

slides.title: AAS Rule (Angle-Angle-Side)
slides.storyContext: Akshay draws AAS: Angle 40°, Angle 70°, and a non-included Side 8 cm. He draws the same for another triangle. 'Both triangles have the same two angles and a side NOT between them. Are they congruent?' Yes — AAS guarantees it.

example.problem: Triangle R: Angle 40°, Angle 70°, Side 8 cm (not between angles). Triangle S: Angle 40°, Angle 70°, Side 8 cm (not between angles). Congruent?
example.solution: Yes, by AAS. Two angles and a non-included side match.

slides.inSimpleWords: AAS is like ASA but the side is NOT between the angles.

slides.title: Congruent Polygons

points.text: For any polygon (triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, etc.) to be congruent, all sides must be equal and all angles must be equal.
Two squares with the same side length are always congruent.
Two rectangles with the same length and width are congruent.

example.problem: Square A has a side of 4 cm. Square B has a side of 4 cm. Square C has a side of 5 cm. Which squares are congruent?
example.solution: Squares A and B are congruent (both have 4 cm sides). Square C is not congruent to A or B.

slides.inSimpleWords: Polygons with matching sides and angles are twins in geometry.

slides.title: Rectangle Congruence
slides.storyContext: Isha finds two rectangular photo frames. Frame 1: 20 cm long, 15 cm wide. Frame 2: 20 cm long, 15 cm wide.

example.problem: Are the frames congruent?
example.solution: Yes. Both have matching length (20 cm) and width (15 cm). All angles in both are 90°, so they are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two rectangles with the same length and width are congruent — all angles are 90° anyway.

slides.title: Reflection and Congruence

points.text: When you flip a shape over a line (called reflection), the new shape is congruent to the original.
The original and reflected shapes are mirror images.
All measurements stay the same; only position and orientation change.

example.problem: Isha reflects a triangle over a vertical line. Is the reflected triangle congruent to the original?
example.solution: Yes. Reflection preserves size and shape, so congruence is maintained.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mirrors create congruent twins — a reflection of a shape is the same shape, just flipped.

slides.title: The Mirror Trick
slides.storyContext: Isha places a triangle against a mirror and sees its reflection. 'Akshay, the reflected triangle looks different, but is it the same?' Akshay replies: 'Measure it. The reflected triangle is congruent — same size and shape, just flipped like a mirror image.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Reflections preserve congruence — the mirror image is congruent to the original.

slides.title: Rotation and Congruence

points.text: When you rotate a shape around a point, the new shape is congruent to the original.
You can rotate by any amount (90°, 180°, 270°, etc.), and congruence is still true.
Only position and orientation change; size and shape stay the same.

example.problem: A square is rotated 45° around its center. Is it congruent to the original square?
example.solution: Yes. Rotation preserves size and shape, so congruence is maintained.

slides.inSimpleWords: Spin a shape, and it remains congruent to itself — just tilted differently.

slides.title: Rotation in Action
slides.storyContext: Isha rotates a star shape 90° clockwise. The star looks tilted now, but is it congruent?

example.problem: A star is rotated 90° clockwise. Are the original and rotated stars congruent?
example.solution: Yes. Rotation preserves size and shape. The rotated star is congruent to the original.

slides.inSimpleWords: No matter how much you rotate a shape, it remains congruent to itself.

slides.title: Translation and Congruence

points.text: Translation means moving a shape from one place to another without rotating or flipping it.
A translated shape is always congruent to the original.
Moving a triangle 5 cm to the right keeps it congruent.

example.problem: A triangle is moved 10 cm to the left. Is it congruent to the original?
example.solution: Yes. Translation preserves size and shape, so the moved triangle is congruent to the original.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sliding a shape (translation) does not change congruence — it stays identical.

slides.title: Isha's Photo Frame Problem
slides.storyContext: Isha has a rectangular photo frame that is 20 cm long and 15 cm wide. She buys another frame and measures it: 15 cm long and 20 cm wide. Are the frames congruent?

example.problem: Frame 1: length 20 cm, width 15 cm. Frame 2: length 15 cm, width 20 cm. Are they congruent?
example.solution: If Frame 2 is rotated 90°, its dimensions match Frame 1 (both 20×15). Yes, they are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: Shapes are congruent even if one is rotated — just check if rotating makes them match.

slides.title: Isha Tests Her Friends
slides.storyContext: Isha shows her friends two quadrilaterals. Quadrilateral A: sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, all angles 90°. Quadrilateral B: rotated 180°, sides 5 cm, 6 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, all angles 90°. 'Are these congruent?' asks Isha. Her friends check: 'Yes! Rotation doesn't matter if the sides and angles match.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Transformations like rotation, reflection, and translation do not destroy congruence.

slides.title: Identifying Congruent Figures with Transformations
slides.storyContext: Isha draws a pentagon and applies multiple transformations: first rotating it 90°, then translating it 10 cm to the right. 'Is this shape still congruent to the original?' Akshay confirms: 'Yes! All transformations preserve congruence.'

example.problem: A shape undergoes rotation (90°), then translation (5 cm right). Is the final shape congruent to the original?
example.solution: Yes. Each transformation individually preserves congruence, so multiple transformations also preserve congruence.

slides.inSimpleWords: Chain transformations together — congruence is preserved through all of them.

slides.title: Identifying Congruent Figures

points.text: Step 1: Compare all side lengths.
Step 2: Compare all angles.
Step 3: If all sides and all angles match, the figures are congruent.
Transformations (rotation, reflection, translation) do not affect congruence.

example.problem: Figure A: triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and angles 30°, 60°, 90°. Figure B: triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 and angles 30°, 60°, 90°. Congruent?
example.solution: Yes. All sides match and all angles match. The figures are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: To check congruence: match sides, match angles, done!

slides.title: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Figures

points.text: When two figures are congruent, their corresponding sides are equal.
Corresponding angles are also equal.
Example: If Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle DEF, then AB = DE, BC = EF, CA = FD, and angles A = D, B = E, C = F.

example.problem: Triangle ABC ≅ Triangle XYZ. If AB = 5 cm, BC = 7 cm, and angle B = 60°, what are XY, YZ, and angle Y?
example.solution: XY = 5 cm, YZ = 7 cm, angle Y = 60°. Corresponding parts are equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: In congruent shapes, corresponding sides and angles match perfectly.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Akshay draws two triangles on paper. Triangle 1 has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and an included angle of 50°. Triangle 2 has sides 6 cm, 8 cm, and the angle between those sides is also 50°. Are they congruent? Then he reflects Triangle 1 over a line. Is the reflection congruent to Triangle 2?

example.problem: Two triangles with SAS (6 cm, 50°, 8 cm) are congruent. If one is reflected, is it still congruent to the other?
example.solution: Yes, both original triangles are congruent (by SAS). After reflection, the reflected triangle is still congruent to both originals.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the rules (SSS, SAS, ASA) to prove congruence, and remember reflections keep congruence.

image.alt: Can You Solve This? — Geometric Twins

slides.title: Advanced Challenge
slides.storyContext: Isha has Triangle ABC with sides AB = 7 cm, BC = 9 cm, CA = 5 cm. She also has Triangle DEF. After measuring, she finds DE = 7 cm, EF = 9 cm, FD = 5 cm. She then rotates Triangle DEF 180° and reflects it. Is the transformed Triangle DEF congruent to Triangle ABC?

example.problem: Two triangles have matching side lengths. After transformation (rotation + reflection), are they still congruent to each other?
example.solution: Yes. Original triangles are congruent by SSS. Rotation and reflection preserve congruence, so the transformed triangle is still congruent to Triangle ABC.

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiple transformations stacked together still preserve congruence.

slides.title: Congruence Proof Challenge
slides.storyContext: Isha receives a complex challenge: Given quadrilateral PQRS with sides 4 cm, 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm and angles 80°, 100°, 90°, 90°. Given quadrilateral TUVW with matching sides and angles in the same order. Prove they are congruent.

example.problem: Two quadrilaterals have all matching sides and angles. Are they congruent?
example.solution: Yes. All four sides match and all four angles match. The quadrilaterals are congruent.

slides.inSimpleWords: For any polygon, equal sides and angles mean congruence.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Two figures are congruent if they have the same size and shape.
For triangles: SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS are the congruence rules.
For polygons, all sides and angles must match.
Reflection, rotation, and translation preserve congruence.
Congruent shapes are geometric twins — identical copies.

slides.inSimpleWords: Congruence is the geometry word for 'identical twins' — same size, same shape, every time.

subject: Mathematics
title: The Temperature Game
hook: Ravi tracks temperature changes in Delhi using positive and negative numbers, then learns to add, subtract, multiply, and divide them.

slides.title: The Temperature Game
slides.storyContext: In Delhi, winter temperatures drop below zero. Ravi and his grandfather use integers to track these changes.

slides.title: Below Zero
slides.storyContext: It's December in Delhi. Grandfather shows Ravi a thermometer. 'See, beta? Today it is 15°C. Yesterday was 8°C. But in January, it will drop to −2°C or even −5°C.' Ravi frowns. 'How can temperature be negative?' Grandfather smiles. 'It is just a number below zero. Let me teach you how integers work — they are positive, negative, and zero.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Integers are whole numbers that can be positive (above zero), negative (below zero), or zero itself.

slides.title: What are Integers?

points.text: Integers are whole numbers: ..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
Positive integers are greater than zero: 1, 2, 3, ...
Negative integers are less than zero: −1, −2, −3, ...
Zero is neither positive nor negative.

example.problem: Write the temperature changes in Delhi as integers. Morning: 10°C. Evening: −3°C. Night: −8°C.
example.solution: Morning = 10. Evening = −3. Night = −8. All are integers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Integers are numbers on a number line: negatives on the left of zero, positives on the right.

slides.title: The Number Line Adventure
slides.storyContext: Grandfather draws a number line. 'Ravi, this line shows all integers. Zero is in the middle. Positives go right, negatives go left. Positive 5 is 5 steps to the right. Negative 5 is 5 steps to the left.' Ravi visualizes marching along the line.
slides.inSimpleWords: The number line is a visual way to understand positive and negative integers.

slides.title: Absolute Value

points.text: Absolute value is the distance from zero on the number line, always positive.
Denoted by |x|. Example: |−5| = 5, |5| = 5.
It tells you 'how far' a number is from zero, regardless of direction.

example.problem: Find |−7| and |7|.
example.solution: |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7. Both are 7 steps away from zero.

slides.inSimpleWords: Absolute value ignores the sign and tells you distance from zero.

slides.title: Adding Integers

points.text: When adding two positive integers: add them normally. 3 + 5 = 8.
When adding two negative integers: add their absolute values and put a negative sign. (−3) + (−5) = −8.
When adding a positive and a negative: find the difference and keep the sign of the larger absolute value. 3 + (−5) = −2.

example.problem: The temperature was 5°C. It dropped 12°C. What is the new temperature?
example.solution: 5 + (−12) = −7. The new temperature is −7°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding a negative is like moving left on the number line; adding positive moves right.

slides.title: Adding Positives and Negatives
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices: Start at +3. Add −5. Where do we end up?

example.solution: Start at 3, move 5 steps left: 3 → 2 → 1 → 0 → −1 → −2. Answer: −2.

slides.inSimpleWords: When adding a negative, move left on the number line.

slides.title: Subtracting Integers

points.text: Subtraction of integers can be rewritten as addition of the opposite. a − b = a + (−b).
Remember: subtracting a negative is like adding a positive.

example.problem: The temperature was −5°C. It rose by 12°C. What is the new temperature?
example.solution: (−5) − (−12) = (−5) + 12 = 7. The new temperature is 7°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Subtraction of integers is really addition of the opposite number.

slides.title: The Subtraction Trick
slides.storyContext: Grandfather tells Ravi: 'Subtraction is a trick! To subtract, just add the opposite. Subtracting −5 is the same as adding +5. Makes sense?' Ravi nods as he understands the pattern.
slides.inSimpleWords: Subtract by adding the opposite — it's a shortcut to make math easier.

slides.title: Adding Two Negatives

points.text: When both integers are negative, add their absolute values and keep the negative sign.
Think of it as losing money twice — you end up more in debt.

example.problem: The temperature dropped 3°C, then dropped another 4°C. What is the total change?
example.solution: (−3) + (−4) = −7. Total drop is 7°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: Adding two negatives gives a bigger negative.

slides.title: Multiplying Integers

points.text: Positive × Positive = Positive. 3 × 5 = 15.
Negative × Negative = Positive. (−3) × (−5) = 15.
Positive × Negative = Negative. 3 × (−5) = −15.
Negative × Positive = Negative. (−3) × 5 = −15.

example.problem: The temperature drops 3°C every hour for 5 hours. What is the total change?
example.solution: (−3) × 5 = −15. The temperature has dropped 15°C.

slides.inSimpleWords: When multiplying integers: same signs give positive; different signs give negative.

slides.title: Multiplication Practice
slides.storyContext: Ravi multiplies (−4) × (−3). Two negatives multiplying together.

example.solution: Negative × Negative = Positive. (−4) × (−3) = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two negatives make a positive — remember this key rule.

slides.title: Dividing Integers

points.text: The rules for division are the same as multiplication.
Positive ÷ Positive = Positive. 15 ÷ 3 = 5.
Negative ÷ Negative = Positive. (−15) ÷ (−3) = 5.
Positive ÷ Negative = Negative. 15 ÷ (−3) = −5.
Negative ÷ Positive = Negative. (−15) ÷ 3 = −5.

example.problem: Over 5 hours, the temperature dropped 20°C. What is the average drop per hour?
example.solution: (−20) ÷ 5 = −4. The average drop is 4°C per hour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Division of integers follows the same positive/negative rules as multiplication.

slides.title: Division with Negatives
slides.storyContext: Ravi divides (−24) ÷ (−4). Two negatives dividing.

example.solution: Negative ÷ Negative = Positive. (−24) ÷ (−4) = 6.

slides.inSimpleWords: Division follows multiplication rules — two negatives give positive.

slides.title: Temperature Drops Over Days
slides.storyContext: Ravi tracks a temperature drop. If the total drop over 3 days is −15°C, what is the average drop per day? Grandfather guides: '−15 ÷ 3 = −5. Each day dropped 5°C.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Division finds the per-unit rate — useful for averaging changes.

slides.title: Order of Operations with Integers (PEMDAS)

points.text: Follow PEMDAS: Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division (left to right), Addition/Subtraction (left to right).
Example: 5 + 3 × (−2) = 5 + (−6) = −1. (Multiply before adding.)
Example: (−8 + 3) × 2 = (−5) × 2 = −10. (Parentheses first.)

example.problem: Calculate: 10 − 2 × (−3) + 4.

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow the order: Parentheses → Exponents → Multiply/Divide → Add/Subtract.

slides.title: Multi-Step Integer Operations
slides.storyContext: Ravi practices a complex calculation: (−5) × 2 + 8 ÷ (−4). He carefully follows order of operations.
slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply and divide first (left to right), then add and subtract.

slides.title: A Week of Temperature Changes
slides.storyContext: Ravi records: Monday +2°, Tuesday −3°, Wednesday −1°, Thursday +4°, Friday −2°. He adds them step by step to find the week's net change.
slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world problems often need multiple operations in sequence.

slides.title: Grandfather's Weather Challenge
slides.storyContext: Grandfather gives Ravi a puzzle: 'Monday was 8°C. Tuesday dropped 12°C. Wednesday rose 5°C. Then we had 4 nights each losing 3°C. What was the temperature after those 4 nights?'

example.problem: Calculate: Start at 8. Subtract 12. Add 5. Subtract (3 × 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine operations step by step: add the positives, add the negatives, then find the difference.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Ravi's weather diary: Monday was −3°C. Over 6 days, the temperature changed by: +2, −4, +1, −5, +3, −2 (in °C each day). What is the final temperature?

example.problem: Start: −3. Changes: +2, −4, +1, −5, +3, −2. Final temperature?

slides.inSimpleWords: Group positive and negative changes, then combine to find the final result.

slides.title: Advanced Challenge: Mixed Operations
slides.storyContext: Ravi faces a complex problem: Start at −5°C. Double the temperature (multiply by 2), then add 8. What is the result?

example.solution: First multiply: (−5) × 2 = −10. Then add: −10 + 8 = −2.

slides.inSimpleWords: When mixing operations, follow PEMDAS — multiplication and division before addition and subtraction.

slides.title: Complex Integer Puzzle
slides.storyContext: Ravi solves: −20 ÷ (−4) − 3 × 2 + (−6). Multiple operations at once.
slides.inSimpleWords: Handle division and multiplication left to right, then subtraction and addition.

slides.title: Real-World Banking Problem
slides.storyContext: Ravi thinks about money: 'If I start with −100 rupees (debt), earn 50 rupees, then earn another 80 rupees, what's my final balance?'

example.problem: Start: −100. Add 50. Add 80. Final balance?
example.solution: (−100) + 50 + 80 = (−100) + 130 = 30 rupees (positive balance now).

slides.inSimpleWords: Real-world problems like debt and earning use integer addition and subtraction.

slides.title: Properties of Integer Operations

points.text: Commutative Property: a + b = b + a and a × b = b × a (order doesn't matter for + and ×).
Associative Property: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c) (grouping doesn't matter).
Distributive Property: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c.

example.solution: Left: (−3) × 7 = −21. Right: −15 + (−6) = −21. Both equal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Math properties help you simplify and reorganize integer calculations.

slides.title: Using Distributive Property

example.problem: Calculate 6 × (−2 + 3) using the distributive property.

slides.inSimpleWords: Distribute the outside number to each term inside the parentheses.

slides.title: Comparing and Ordering Integers

points.text: Integers on a number line increase from left to right.
−5 < −2 < 0 < 3 < 7 (less than relationships).
Use < (less than), > (greater than), = (equal) to compare.

example.problem: Order from smallest to largest: −5, 0, 3, −2, 7.

slides.inSimpleWords: On the number line, left is smaller; right is larger.

slides.title: Comparing Integer Temperatures
slides.storyContext: Ravi compares winter temperatures: −8°C vs −3°C. Which is colder?

example.problem: Which is colder: −8°C or −3°C?
example.solution: −8°C is colder because −8 < −3 (further left on the number line).

slides.inSimpleWords: More negative means colder — further left on the number line.

slides.title: Multi-Step Real-World Challenge
slides.storyContext: Ravi's bank account started at −50 rupees. He earned 200 rupees, spent 75 rupees, then earned 120 rupees. What is his final balance?
slides.inSimpleWords: Track income and expenses step by step to find the final balance.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Integers include positive, negative, and zero.
Adding integers: use sign rules (same signs, different signs).
Subtracting integers: convert to addition of the opposite.
Multiplying/dividing integers: same signs give positive; different signs give negative.
Combine operations step by step using order of operations (PEMDAS).

slides.inSimpleWords: Integer operations follow sign rules: positive-positive and negative-negative are positive; mixed signs are negative.

subject: Mathematics
title: Dividing the Harvest
hook: A farmer needs to divide 24 baskets of wheat and 36 baskets of rice equally among workers, and finds the largest group size possible.

slides.title: Dividing the Harvest
slides.storyContext: On a farm in Punjab, Farmer Gopal must distribute grain baskets fairly among workers.

slides.title: The Fair Share
slides.storyContext: Harvest season has arrived. Farmer Gopal has 24 baskets of wheat and 36 baskets of rice. He wants to divide them equally among workers without leaving any baskets unopened or wasting grain. Anita asks: 'Dad, what if we hire 6 workers? Can we divide evenly?' Gopal thinks hard. 'Not sure, beta. Let me find a number that divides both perfectly. That would be fair to everyone.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Finding numbers that divide evenly into two quantities is about finding common factors.

slides.title: Factors and Divisors

points.text: A factor of a number divides it exactly with no remainder.

example.problem: List all factors of 24.
example.solution: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24. Each divides 24 with remainder 0.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factors are numbers that divide evenly into another number with no leftover.

image.alt: Factors and Divisors — Finding Common Ground

slides.title: Anita Tests Factors
slides.storyContext: Anita writes down: 'If Dad has 24 baskets of wheat, he could divide among 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, or 24 workers. All these are factors of 24. With 5 workers, there would be leftover baskets — 5 is not a factor of 24.'
slides.inSimpleWords: A factor divides perfectly; a non-factor leaves remainder.

slides.title: Testing Divisibility

points.text: A number is divisible by 2 if it is even (ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8).
A number is divisible by 3 if the sum of its digits is divisible by 3.
A number is divisible by 5 if it ends in 0 or 5.
These rules help quickly identify factors.

example.problem: Is 36 divisible by 3?
example.solution: Sum of digits: 3 + 6 = 9. Since 9 is divisible by 3, yes, 36 is divisible by 3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Divisibility rules let you quickly check if a number is a factor.

slides.title: Common Factors

points.text: A common factor is a number that divides two or more numbers evenly.
Common factors of 24 and 36: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.
These six numbers divide both 24 and 36 with no remainder.

example.problem: Find common factors of 24 and 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Common factors divide multiple numbers at the same time.

slides.title: Testing Common Factors
slides.storyContext: Anita checks: 'If we hire 6 workers, can we divide both 24 wheat and 36 rice equally? Let's see: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 baskets per worker. 36 ÷ 6 = 6 baskets per worker. Yes! 6 is a common factor.'

example.problem: Is 6 a common factor of 24 and 36?
example.solution: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 (no remainder). 36 ÷ 6 = 6 (no remainder). Yes, 6 is a common factor.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check if a number divides both quantities evenly.

slides.title: Greatest Common Factor (GCF)

points.text: The Greatest Common Factor (GCF) is the largest number that divides two or more numbers evenly.
GCF of 24 and 36 is 12 (the largest common factor).
If we divide both by their GCF: 24 ÷ 12 = 2, and 36 ÷ 12 = 3.

example.problem: Find the GCF of 24 and 36.
example.solution: Common factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. The greatest is 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF is the biggest number that divides both quantities evenly.

image.alt: Greatest Common Factor (GCF) — Finding Common Ground

slides.title: Finding the Maximum Workers
slides.storyContext: Anita declares: 'Dad, the GCF of 24 and 36 is 12. That means you can hire 12 workers, and each gets exactly 2 baskets of wheat and 3 baskets of rice. That's the fairest way!' Gopal smiles: 'Perfect, beta!'
slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF tells us the maximum number of equal groups we can make.

slides.title: Finding GCF Using Prime Factorization

points.text: Prime factorization breaks a number into prime factors (numbers only divisible by 1 and themselves).
GCF = 2² × 3 = 12 (take the lowest power of each common prime).

example.problem: Find GCF of 24 and 36 using prime factorization.
example.solution: 24 = 2³ × 3. 36 = 2² × 3². Common primes: 2² and 3¹. GCF = 2² × 3 = 4 × 3 = 12.

slides.inSimpleWords: Prime factorization shows which primes are shared; multiply the shared ones (in lowest power) to get the GCF.

slides.title: Prime Factorization Practice
slides.storyContext: Anita draws a factor tree for 36. She breaks it down: 36 = 6 × 6 = (2 × 3) × (2 × 3) = 2² × 3².

example.problem: Find the prime factorization of 36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Break a number into prime factors by repeatedly dividing by primes.

slides.title: Using GCF to Simplify Fractions

points.text: The GCF helps us simplify fractions and divide quantities fairly.
To reduce a fraction: divide both numerator and denominator by their GCF.

example.problem: Simplify 18/30.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing both top and bottom by their GCF makes a fraction simpler.

slides.title: Simplifying Gopal's Ratio
slides.storyContext: Anita simplifies the ratio of wheat to rice: 24 to 36. Using the GCF of 12: 24/36 = 2/3. So each worker gets 2 wheat to 3 rice — a 2:3 ratio.

example.problem: Simplify the ratio 24:36.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ratios can be simplified using the GCF.

slides.title: Gopal's Worker Distribution
slides.storyContext: Farmer Gopal decides to use the GCF. He has 24 baskets of wheat and 36 baskets of rice. He wants to hire the maximum number of workers such that each gets an equal share.

example.problem: If Gopal uses the GCF to divide, how many workers should he hire? How many baskets of wheat and rice does each get?
example.solution: GCF of 24 and 36 is 12. So hire 12 workers. Each gets 24 ÷ 12 = 2 baskets of wheat and 36 ÷ 12 = 3 baskets of rice.

slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF tells us the maximum number of equal groups we can make.

slides.title: Finding GCF Using the Euclidean Algorithm

points.text: The Euclidean algorithm repeatedly divides the larger number by the smaller.
Replace the larger with the smaller, and the smaller with the remainder.
When remainder is 0, the other number is the GCF.

example.problem: Find GCF(48, 18) using the Euclidean algorithm.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Euclidean algorithm is a fast way to find GCF by repeated division.

slides.title: Can You Solve This?
slides.storyContext: Anita's school has 48 red pens and 60 blue pens. The teacher wants to pack them into identical gift boxes, with no pens left over and no mixing of colors. What is the maximum number of boxes the teacher can make? How many red and blue pens go in each box?

example.problem: Find GCF of 48 and 60, then determine box count and contents.
example.solution: GCF of 48 and 60 is 12. So 12 boxes. Each box has 48 ÷ 12 = 4 red pens and 60 ÷ 12 = 5 blue pens.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the GCF to find the maximum number of equal groups (boxes).

slides.title: Advanced Challenge: Multiple Groups
slides.storyContext: Gopal now has 40 apples, 60 oranges, and 80 mangoes. He wants to pack them into identical boxes with no fruit left over. What is the GCF, and how many boxes can he make?

example.problem: Find GCF of 40, 60, and 80.
example.solution: 40 = 2³ × 5, 60 = 2² × 3 × 5, 80 = 2⁴ × 5. GCF = 2² × 5 = 20. He can make 20 boxes. Each has 2 apples, 3 oranges, 4 mangoes.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCF works for three or more numbers too — find the common prime factors with lowest powers.

slides.title: Real-World GCF Challenge
slides.storyContext: A community center has 72 sport balls and 90 cones. They want to create identical sports kits with no equipment left over. What is the maximum number of kits? How many balls and cones in each?

example.problem: Find GCF of 72 and 90, then determine kit count and contents.
example.solution: 72 = 2³ × 3². 90 = 2 × 3² × 5. GCF = 2 × 3² = 18. So 18 kits. Each has 72 ÷ 18 = 4 balls and 90 ÷ 18 = 5 cones.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCF solves real fair-sharing problems in sports, classrooms, and community settings.

slides.title: Least Common Multiple (LCM)

points.text: The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest number divisible by two or more numbers.
LCM of 6 and 8: Multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, ... Multiples of 8 are 8, 16, 24, ... LCM = 24.
LCM is useful for finding common denominators in fractions.

example.problem: Find LCM of 6 and 8.
example.solution: Multiples of 6: 6, 12, 18, 24. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. LCM = 24.

slides.inSimpleWords: The LCM is the smallest number that both numbers divide into evenly.

slides.title: LCM in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Gopal's buses arrive: one every 6 days, another every 8 days. When will they both arrive on the same day?

example.problem: Find LCM of 6 and 8 to determine when buses arrive together.
example.solution: LCM of 6 and 8 is 24. The buses will arrive together every 24 days.

slides.inSimpleWords: LCM helps solve scheduling and repeated-event problems.

slides.title: LCM Using Prime Factorization

points.text: To find LCM: list prime factors of each number and take the HIGHEST power of each prime.
Compare to GCF: GCF uses lowest powers; LCM uses highest powers.

example.problem: Find LCM of 12 and 18 using prime factorization.

slides.inSimpleWords: For LCM, multiply the highest power of each prime factor.

slides.title: GCF vs LCM Comparison
slides.storyContext: Anita notices: GCF and LCM are related opposites. GCF finds the biggest shared divisor; LCM finds the smallest shared multiple.

example.problem: For 24 and 36: find both GCF and LCM.
example.solution: GCF = 12 (biggest divisor of both). LCM = 72 (smallest multiple of both). Note: 12 × 72 = 24 × 36 = 864.

slides.inSimpleWords: GCF ÷ into; LCM × into — opposite operations.

slides.title: Coprime Numbers

points.text: Two numbers are coprime (or relatively prime) if their GCF is 1.
Example: 15 and 28 are coprime (GCF = 1).
Coprime numbers share no common factors except 1.

example.problem: Are 15 and 28 coprime?
example.solution: Factors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15. Factors of 28: 1, 2, 4, 7, 14, 28. Only common factor is 1. Yes, coprime.

slides.inSimpleWords: Coprime numbers have nothing in common except 1.

slides.title: Real-World Fraction Simplification
slides.storyContext: Anita needs to simplify 28/42. She finds GCF(28, 42) = 14, so 28/42 = 2/3.

example.problem: Simplify 28/42.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCF to reduce fractions to simplest form.

slides.title: GCF and LCM Combined Challenge
slides.storyContext: Gopal has two tasks: Pack 30 red ribbons and 45 blue ribbons into boxes (GCF problem). Schedule two workers who work every 20 days and 30 days (LCM problem).

example.problem: Find GCF(30, 45) for boxes. Find LCM(20, 30) for scheduling.
example.solution: GCF(30, 45) = 15 boxes. LCM(20, 30) = 60 days until both work together again.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use GCF for dividing groups; use LCM for synchronizing schedules.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: A factor divides a number evenly with no remainder.
A common factor divides two or more numbers evenly.
The GCF is the greatest common factor — the largest number dividing all given numbers.
Prime factorization and division methods both find the GCF.
The GCF simplifies fractions, finds equal distributions, and solves real-world fair-sharing problems.

slides.inSimpleWords: The GCF is the key to dividing quantities fairly and simplifying fractions.
